title: Bēowulf
titleEn: Beowulf — Fitt XII: The Arm Torn Away (lines 791–836)
part: Fitt XII · The Arm Torn Away (lines 791–836)
source: Fr. Klaeber, Beowulf and the Fight at Finnsburg, 1st edition (Boston: D. C. Heath & Co., 1922), pp. 30–32, lines 791–836 (fitt XII). Text follows Klaeber's printing exactly — þ, ð, æ, vowel-length macrons, a circumflex for contracted vowels (Klaeber prints one mark over the pair of vowels; we place it on the second), [brackets] for letters or words added by emendation, (parentheses) for conjectural restoration of fire-damaged letters, and Klaeber's rows of dots where words are lost. A dot under a vowel (dōgọra) is Klaeber's sign that the vowel does not count in the metre. Transcribed from the page images of the archive.org scan, every page read twice. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed late West Saxon, c. 1000, following Campbell's Old English Grammar — and the recorded reading follows it, within stated limits. No synthetic voice for Old English exists, so the reading is produced by an American English neural voice under per-word phonetic pinning: every sound is specified outright rather than left to modern English habits. So æ is the vowel of 'cat' and a the open back vowel of 'father'; short and long vowels stay apart; ea and eo are sounded as two-part diphthongs; sc is 'sh', cg the 'j' of 'edge', hw a breathy w; h after a vowel is the rasp of German 'ach' or 'ich'; and doubled consonants are held long. The limits: the voice has no throaty g (dagas, lagu), so it says a plain g; long ǣ, long ȳ and long ēa are heard short; compounds are not split, so a sound at the seam of a compound is occasionally voiced where it should not be; and unstressed vowels keep their full quality. The reading is a model of one scholarly convention, as much a reconstruction as the text. Translations made fresh from the original.
about: Beowulf survives in a single manuscript, the Nowell Codex, which was scorched in a library fire in 1731; its edges have crumbled away, and some readings survive only in two transcripts made in 1787. What you read here is a reconstruction — Klaeber's edition of 1922 — and parts of it are educated guesswork: [brackets] mark letters editors added, (parentheses) mark letters restored where the manuscript is damaged or lost, and a few words are best guesses whose exact meaning no one knows. The notes say so where it matters. Line numbers are Klaeber's, the standard way of citing the poem.

sentences.t:
Nolde eorla hlēo ǣnige þinga
þone cwealmcuman cwicne forlǣtan,
nē his līfdagas lēoda ǣnigum
nytte tealde.
sentences.l: Would not the shelter of earls, on any account, the death-comer alive let go, nor his life-days to any of the peoples of use reckoned.
sentences.i: The protector of earls would not on any account let the death-bringer go alive, nor did he count that one’s days of life of any use to any of the peoples.
sentences.n: ‘Nolde’ is ‘ne wolde’, ‘would not’, and its subject is ‘eorla hlēo’, ‘shelter of earls’, Beowulf, who still holds Grendel from the fitt before; the same ‘hlēo’ is ‘wīgendra hlēo’, ‘shelter of warriors’, at 429. ‘ǣnige þinga’ is ‘in any of things’, a fixed phrase for ‘on any account’. ‘cwealmcuman’ is ‘cwealm’, ‘death’, and ‘cuma’, ‘comer’, so ‘death-comer’, and ‘cwicne’ is accusative masculine, ‘alive’. In the second clause ‘nē’ is ‘nor’, ‘his’ is Grendel’s, ‘nytte’ is ‘of use’, either the noun ‘nytt’, ‘use’, or the adjective ‘nytt’, ‘useful’, agreeing with ‘līfdagas’ (the sense is the same), and ‘tealde’ is the past of ‘tellan’, ‘count, reckon’; ‘lēoda ǣnigum’ is ‘to any of the peoples’. The clause also tells us that Grendel’s life was worth nothing to anyone.

sentences.t:
Þǣr genehost brægd
eorl Bēowulfes ealde lāfe,
wolde frēadrihtnes feorh ealgian,
mǣres þēodnes, ðǣr hīe meahton swā.
sentences.l: There very often drew Beowulf’s earl the old leaving, wished the master-lord’s life to defend, the famed lord’s, where they could do so.
sentences.i: There many a man of Beowulf’s drew his old heirloom blade again and again, wishing to defend the life of their master, that famed lord, if they could.
sentences.n: ‘eorl Bēowulfes’ is singular but means the whole band, a collective, and ‘hīe meahton’ at the end is plural, which shows it; so I give ‘many a man of Beowulf’s’. ‘genehost’ is a superlative adverb, ‘most abundantly’, and I take it as ‘very often’. ‘brægd’ is the past of ‘bregdan’, ‘draw, brandish’. ‘ealde lāfe’ is ‘the old leaving’, an accusative singular feminine and the object of ‘brægd’ (‘ealde’ could not be a dative, which would be ‘ealdre’): ‘lāf’ is what is left behind by the fathers, so an heirloom, and by the sense a sword. ‘frēadrihtnes’ is ‘frēa’, ‘lord’, and ‘dryhten’, ‘ruler’, and ‘mǣres þēodnes’ is a genitive in apposition. ‘ðǣr hīe meahton swā’ is ‘where they could do so’, ‘if they were able’. The Geats have drawn swords and cannot help.

sentences.t:
Hīe þæt ne wiston, þā hīe gewin drugon,
heardhicgende hildemecgas,
ond on healfa gehwone hēawan þōhton,
sāwle sēcan:
sentences.l: They that did not know, when they carried on the struggle, the hard-minded battle-men, and on each of sides thought to hew, to seek the soul:
sentences.i: They did not know this, those hard-minded fighters, when they were waging the struggle and thought to hew at him from every side and seek out his soul:
sentences.n: ‘Hīe þæt ne wiston’ is ‘they did not know that’: ‘wiston’ is the past plural of ‘witan’, and ‘þæt’ points forward to the clause after the colon. ‘þā hīe gewin drugon’ is ‘when they carried on the struggle’: ‘drugon’ is the past plural of ‘drēogan’, ‘endure, perform’, and ‘gewin’ is ‘strife’. ‘heardhicgende’ is ‘hard-minded’, a present participle (compare fitt VI), and ‘hildemecgas’ is ‘battle-men’, from ‘hilde’, ‘battle’, and ‘mecg’, ‘man’. ‘on healfa gehwone’ is ‘on every side’, literally ‘on each of sides’. ‘hēawan’ and ‘sēcan’ follow ‘þōhton’, ‘thought, meant’; ‘sāwle sēcan’, ‘to seek the soul’, means to kill him.

sentences.l: That sin-scather any over earth, best of irons, of war-bills none, would not greet;
sentences.i: No blade on earth, not the best of irons, not one war-sword, would touch that sinful marauder;
sentences.n: ‘þone synscaðan’ is the object, put first; the subject comes after it, ‘ǣnig … īrenna cyst, gūðbilla nān’, ‘any, the best of irons, of war-bills none’. ‘Nolde’ is ‘would not’, so the negative sits in the verb; Old English often piles up ‘any’ and ‘none’ with it and means ‘none’. ‘īrenna’ is a genitive plural of ‘īren’, ‘iron’, used for ‘sword’; a ‘gūðbill’ is a ‘war-bill’, a sword. ‘grētan’ is ‘greet’ and here means ‘touch, attack’. ‘synscaðan’ is ‘syn’, ‘sin’, and ‘scaða’, ‘harmer’; I take ‘syn’ as ‘sin’, but the prefix may mean ‘huge’ or ‘lasting’, as in ‘synsnǣdum’ (743), so that part is a guess. The weapons are made to seem unwilling.

sentences.t:
ac hē sigewǣpnum forsworen hæfde,
ecga gehwylcre.
sentences.l: but he had forsworn victory-weapons, each of edges.
sentences.i: but he had put every victory-weapon under a ban, every edge.
sentences.n: ‘hē … forsworen hæfde’ is ‘he had forsworn’, a perfect made from ‘habban’ and the past participle of ‘forswerian’; the verb takes a dative, ‘sigewǣpnum’, ‘victory-weapons’, with ‘ecga gehwylcre’, ‘each of edges’, repeating it. ‘forswerian’ usually means ‘swear falsely’ or ‘renounce on oath’, and the sense I give, that he had put all blades under a ban by oath so that they would not bite, is a guess from the context; the line after it does not say who swore. ‘ecga’ is a genitive plural of ‘ecg’, ‘edge, sword’. The poet gives this as the reason why the swords failed.

sentences.t:
Scolde his aldorgedāl
on ðǣm dæge þysses līfes
earmlīc wurðan, ond se ellorgāst
on fēonda geweald feor sīðian. —
sentences.l: Should his life-parting on that day of this life wretched become, and the elsewhere-ghost far journey into the fiends’ power.
sentences.i: On that day his departure from this life was to be wretched, and his spirit, bound elsewhere, was to journey far into the power of fiends.
sentences.n: ‘Scolde … wurðan’ is ‘was to become’: ‘scolde’ is the past of ‘sculan’, ‘must, be fated’, and ‘wurðan’ is ‘weorþan’, ‘become’. ‘aldorgedāl’ is ‘aldor’, ‘life’, and ‘gedāl’, ‘parting’, so ‘life-parting’, death (compare ‘aldordagum’, ‘life-days’, at 718). ‘earmlīc’ is ‘wretched’. ‘on ðǣm dæge þysses līfes’ is the phrase at 790, there ‘in those days’; here it is the day of his death. ‘ellorgāst’ is ‘ellor’, ‘elsewhere’, and ‘gāst’, ‘spirit’, the spirit that goes to another place. ‘on fēonda geweald’ is ‘into the fiends’ power’, with ‘on’ and the accusative, which gives motion. ‘sīðian’ is ‘journey’, as at 720. The dash after it closes the paragraph.

sentences.t:
Ðā þæt onfunde sē þe fela ǣror
mōdes myrðe manna cynne,
fyrene gefremede — hē fāg wið God —,
þæt him se līchoma lǣstan nolde,
ac hine se mōdẹga mǣg Hygelāces
hæfde be honda;
sentences.l: Then that found out he who, much before, from mind’s mirth, to the kin of men had done crimes — he was hostile to God —, that to him the body would not perform, but him Higelac’s high-spirited kinsman had by the hand;
sentences.i: Then he who long before had done crimes to mankind, in the joy of his heart (he was God’s enemy), found out that his body would not serve him, but Higelac’s high-spirited kinsman had him by the hand;
sentences.n: ‘Ðā þæt onfunde sē þe …’ is ‘then he who … found out that’, with ‘þæt’ looking ahead to the clause ‘þæt him se līchoma lǣstan nolde’, ‘that the body would not perform for him’ (‘līchoma’ is ‘body’, literally ‘body-covering’). ‘mōdes myrðe’ I take as ‘in mind’s mirth’, with relish; this is a guess, and Gering emends ‘mōdes’ to ‘morðres’, ‘of murder’. ‘hē fāg wið God’ has no verb: Klaeber leaves it out, and four editors add ‘wæs’. ‘fāg’ is ‘hostile, guilty’. ‘mōdẹga’ has the first dot under a vowel in this part: Klaeber’s sign that the vowel does not count in the metre, so the word presumably scans as ‘mōdga’. ‘mǣg Hygelāces’ is ‘Higelac’s kinsman’, as at 407 and 736.

sentences.l: was each to the other, living, hateful.
sentences.i: each of them, while he lived, was hateful to the other.
sentences.n: ‘gehwæþer’ is ‘each of two’, the subject, and ‘ōðrum lāð’ is ‘hateful to the other’, ‘ōðrum’ a dative. ‘lifigende’ is a present participle, ‘living’, a nominative singular, so it agrees with ‘gehwæþer’ and not with the dative ‘ōðrum’: ‘each, so long as he lived’. ‘lāð’ is ‘hateful, loathed’, the same word as ‘lāðan’ for Grendel in the second fitt, and it is plain here that the hatred runs both ways.

sentences.l: Body-sore endured the terrible awesome one;
sentences.i: The terrible awesome one suffered bodily pain;
sentences.n: ‘gebād’ is the past of ‘gebīdan’, ‘experience, endure’, and ‘atol ǣglǣca’ is the subject, put after the verb. ‘Līcsār’ is ‘līc’, ‘body’, and ‘sār’, ‘pain’, in the accusative; ‘sār’ is also in ‘sār wānigean’ at 787. ‘ǣglǣca’ is the disputed word that I render ‘awesome one’ throughout, as in fitt II and at 732; it is applied to Grendel and also to heroes, and it seems to mean a terrible opponent. The word is spelled with ‘ǣ’ here and with ‘ā’ in 732; both are Klaeber’s printing.

sentences.t:
him on eaxle wearð
syndolh sweotol, seonowe onsprungon,
burston bānlocan.
sentences.l: to him on shoulder came a huge-wound, plain; sinews sprang apart, bone-locks burst.
sentences.i: A huge wound showed plain on his shoulder; the sinews sprang apart and the joints burst.
sentences.n: ‘him on eaxle wearð syndolh sweotol’ is ‘to him on the shoulder there came a wound, plain’: ‘him’ is a possessive dative, as at 726, ‘wearð’ is the past of ‘weorþan’, ‘become, appear’, and ‘sweotol’ is ‘clear’. ‘syndolh’ is ‘syn-’ and ‘dolg’, ‘wound’; I take the prefix as ‘great’, a guess (in ‘synscaðan’ above I took the same prefix as ‘sin’, so the two renderings differ). ‘seonowe onsprungon’ is ‘sinews sprang apart’: ‘seonowe’ is a plural noun, and ‘onsprungon’ the past plural of ‘onspringan’, ‘spring open’. ‘burston bānlocan’ is ‘the bone-locks burst’: ‘bānlocan’ is the word at 742 that I took for the body’s joints, and here it is the joints of the shoulder. This is Grendel’s arm giving way at the root.

sentences.i: Glory in battle was granted to Beowulf;
sentences.n: ‘Bēowulfe’ is a dative, ‘to Beowulf’, the person who receives, and ‘wearð … gyfeþe’ is ‘was granted’: ‘gyfeþe’ is an adjective, ‘given, granted’, from the verb ‘giefan’, ‘give’, and ‘wearð’ with it makes the passive. The subject is ‘gūðhrēð’, ‘war-glory’, ‘gūð’, ‘battle’, and ‘hrēð’, ‘glory, victory’. The same dative-and-‘wearð’ frame was used of Grendel’s wound just before, and again at 823 of the Danes’ wish; three outcomes are given in the same grammar.

sentences.l: should Grendel from there, life-sick, flee under the fen-slopes, seek a joyless dwelling;
sentences.i: Grendel had to flee from there, sick unto death, under the fen-slopes, and seek his joyless dwelling;
sentences.n: ‘scolde’ governs two infinitives, ‘fleôn’ and ‘sēcean’, ‘had to flee’ and ‘to seek’; the circumflex on ‘fleôn’ is Klaeber’s mark for a contracted vowel. ‘þonan’ is ‘from there’. ‘feorhsēoc’ is ‘feorh’, ‘life’, and ‘sēoc’, ‘sick’, so ‘sick in his life’, mortally hurt. ‘under fenhleoðu’ is ‘under the fen-slopes’, an accusative plural of ‘hleoðu’, the same word as ‘misthleoþum’ at 710. ‘wynlēas wīc’ is ‘joyless dwelling’: ‘wynlēas’ is ‘wyn’, ‘joy’, and ‘-lēas’, ‘without’, and ‘wīc’ is a neuter noun, ‘dwelling, lair’. It echoes ‘drēamum bedǣled’ at 721 as Grendel goes home deprived of joy.

sentences.t:
wiste þē geornor,
þæt his aldres wæs ende gegongen,
dōgera dægrīm.
sentences.l: he knew the more eagerly that of his life the end was come to, the day-count of days.
sentences.i: He knew all the better that the end of his life had come, the count of his days.
sentences.n: ‘wiste’ is the past of ‘witan’, ‘know’; ‘þē geornor’ is ‘by that the more eagerly’, and I take it as ‘all the better’, a guess at an idiom. The ‘þæt’ clause gives what he knew: ‘ende’ is the subject, ‘aldres’ a genitive, ‘of life’, and ‘gegongen’ the past participle of ‘gegangan’, ‘come to pass, arrive’, so ‘the end of his life was come’. ‘dōgera dægrīm’ repeats it, in apposition: ‘dōgera’ is a genitive plural of ‘dōgor’, ‘day’, and ‘dægrīm’ is ‘day-count’, the reckoned number of days.

sentences.t:
Denum eallum wearð
æfter þām wælrǣse willa gelumpen.
sentences.l: To the Danes all came, after the slaughter-rush, the wish fulfilled.
sentences.i: After that rush of slaughter all the Danes had their wish.
sentences.n: ‘wearð … gelumpen’ is ‘came about’, a passive made from ‘weorþan’ and the past participle of ‘gelimpan’, ‘happen, befall’ (compare ‘ālumpen’ at 733); the subject is ‘willa’, ‘wish’, and ‘Denum eallum’ is the dative, ‘to all the Danes’. The same frame ‘Denum eallum wearð’ opened 767, where what came was ‘ealuscerwen’, ‘ale-dealing’, which I took as a bitter fright; here what comes is the Danes’ wish. ‘wælrǣs’ is ‘wæl’, ‘slaughter’, and ‘rǣs’, ‘rush’, so ‘the onrush of killing’, and ‘æfter þām’ is ‘after’, which gives the order of events.

sentences.t:
Hæfde þā gefǣlsod sē þe ǣr feorran cōm
snotor ond swȳðferhð sele Hrōðgāres,
genered wið nīðe.
sentences.l: Had then cleansed, he who before from afar came, wise and strong-spirited, Hrothgar’s hall, saved from malice.
sentences.i: Then he who had come from afar, wise and strong-hearted, had cleansed Hrothgar’s hall and saved it from malice.
sentences.n: ‘Hæfde … gefǣlsod’ is ‘had cleansed’, a perfect made from ‘habban’ and the past participle of ‘gefǣlsian’, ‘cleanse’; its object is ‘sele Hrōðgāres’, ‘Hrothgar’s hall’, and ‘genered’ is a second participle, ‘rescued’, from ‘generian’. The subject is ‘sē þe ǣr feorran cōm’, ‘he who before came from afar’, Beowulf unnamed, with ‘snotor ond swȳðferhð’, ‘wise and strong-spirited’ (‘swȳð’, ‘strong’, ‘ferhð’, ‘spirit’). ‘wið nīðe’ is ‘from malice’, and ‘nīð’ is ‘hostility’, as in ‘wælnīðe’ in the first fitt. Grendel held the hall for twelve winters (147), and at 432 Beowulf asked leave to ‘Heorot fǣlsian’, ‘cleanse Heorot’, so ‘gefǣlsod’ reports that done.

sentences.l: In the night-work he rejoiced, in the courage-glories.
sentences.i: He rejoiced in his night’s work, in his deeds of valour.
sentences.n: ‘gefeh’ is the past of ‘gefēon’, ‘rejoice’, which takes a dative of what one rejoices in: ‘Nihtweorce’, ‘night-work’, and ‘ellenmǣrþum’, a dative plural, ‘glorious deeds of courage’. ‘Nihtweorc’ is ‘niht’, ‘night’, and ‘weorc’, ‘work’; ‘ellenmǣrþum’ is ‘ellen’, ‘courage’, and ‘mǣrþu’, ‘glory, glorious deed’. The subject is still Beowulf, not named. ‘ellen’ is also the first part of ‘ellengǣst’, ‘bold-spirit’, the name given to Grendel at 86.

sentences.t:
Hæfde Ēast-Denum
Gēatmecga lēod gilp gelǣsted,
swylce oncȳþðe ealle gebētte,
inwidsorge, þē hīe ǣr drugon
ond for þrēanȳdum þolian scoldon,
torn unlȳtel.
sentences.l: Had to the East-Danes the Geat-men’s prince his boast fulfilled; likewise all griefs he made good, the malice-sorrow that they before had endured and for dire needs had to suffer, anguish not small.
sentences.i: The prince of the Geat-men had made good his boast to the East-Danes, and likewise he had made amends for all their grief, the sorrow of malice that they had endured before and had been forced to suffer in dire need, anguish not small.
sentences.n: ‘Hæfde … gelǣsted’ is ‘had fulfilled’, with ‘gilp’, ‘boast’, as object; ‘Ēast-Denum’ is a dative of the people helped, and ‘Gēatmecga lēod’, ‘the Geat-men’s prince’, is the subject (‘lēod’ here is a masculine noun, ‘man, prince’; ‘mecg’ is ‘man’). ‘swylce’ is ‘likewise’, and ‘swylce … gebētte’ is a plain past, not a participle, ‘he made good’, from ‘gebētan’, ‘repair’ (my idiomatic line carries the earlier ‘had’ over to it), with ‘oncȳþðe ealle’, ‘all griefs’, and ‘inwidsorge’, ‘malice-sorrow’, as objects. ‘þē hīe ǣr drugon ond … þolian scoldon’ is ‘which they had endured and had to suffer’, ‘þrēanȳdum’ a dative plural, ‘dire need’. ‘torn unlȳtel’ is ‘anguish not little’, in apposition.

sentences.t:
Þæt wæs tācen sweotol,
syþðan hildedēor hond ālegde,
earm ond eaxle — þǣr wæs eal geador
Grendles grāpe — under gēapne hr(ōf).
sentences.l: That was a token plain, after the battle-brave one laid down the hand, arm and shoulder — there was all together Grendel’s grip — under the wide roof.
sentences.i: That was a plain token, after the warrior brave in battle laid down the hand, the arm and the shoulder — there was Grendel’s whole grasp together — under the wide roof.
sentences.n: ‘Þæt wæs tācen sweotol’ is ‘that was a clear token’, and the ‘syþðan’ clause says of what: ‘hildedēor’, ‘battle-brave one’ (compare 312), ‘hond ālegde’, ‘laid down the hand’, with ‘earm ond eaxle’ as further objects. ‘þǣr wæs eal geador Grendles grāpe’ is a parenthesis, ‘there was all together Grendel’s grip’. The punctuation of 835b–836a is disputed: several editors take ‘þǣr wæs eal geador’ (835b) as a clause by itself, ‘there it all was together’, which leaves ‘Grendles grāpe’ as an added phrase. ‘gēapne’ is ‘wide, vaulted’, and ‘wide’ is my guess. ‘hr(ōf)’ is restored: the apparatus gives the manuscript as ‘hr’ and two blanks (I take ‘B’ to be a Thorkelin transcript); Rask and the editors read ‘hrōf’, ‘roof’, and Miller ‘horn’, ‘gable’.
